newsitem.title: USA: Gore to unveil new encryption export policy.
newsitem.headline: Gore to unveil new encryption export policy.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore will release a new policy on Tuesday relaxing export restrictions on computer encoding technology, Gore's office said.
The policy, based on recommendations made in July, is unlikely to satisfy critics in Congress and the computer industry of the current export restrictions on encryption.
Under current law, U.S. companies are allowed to export products containing weak encryption but stronger programs cannot be sold abroad without a special license from the State Department.
Encryption programs use mathematical formulas to scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key."

The administration's plan is expected to raise the length of keys allowed in exported programs to 56 bits from 40 bits. But exporters would have to agree to incorporate so-called key recovery or key escrow features into the programs within two years.
Users of such programs would place duplicate keys in trust with the government or a third party. The government could gain access to the keys with a court order.
And, under the new policy, U.S. companies would be free to sell encryption programs with any key length abroad if the software already included key escrow features.
Critics of the current policy said the new proposal does not go far enough.

"The admininistration needs to work with Congress to develop a consensus on national encryption policy," said Sen. Patrick Leahy, sponsor of a bill in the Senate that would eliminate most export restrictions outright. "Taking unliteral steps will not resolve this issue but instead could delay building the consensus we so urgently need."
The Senate bill, co-sponsored by Montana Republican Conrad Burns, would also prohibit mandatory key escrow.
The computer industry has said it is losing millions of dollars in sales abroad under the current policy.

But U.S. law enforcement officials have said that widely available encryption software would make the job of catching criminals much more difficult and their arguments appear to have carried the day with the administration.
